title: Reinforcement Learning for Control

mentor.name: POLICY-0
mentor.character: Makes you count what the lesson cost the robot before it lets you call the policy good.

summary: You will build tabular reinforcement learning from the reward signal up: returns, discount, value and action value tables, policy and value iteration, Monte Carlo, TD, Q-learning and SARSA on a grid arena. By the end you can train a policy, prove it matches the planned optimum, and put a number on the episodes, the falls and the hours a real robot would have spent learning it.

lessons.title: The Number the Robot Chases
lessons.goal: Write a reward function and add up what a walk through the arena pays.
lessons.theory:
A controller minimises an **error**. You hand it a setpoint, it measures, it subtracts, and the sign of the difference tells it which way to push. A reinforcement learner has no setpoint. It receives one number per step, the **reward**, and that number is not a distance to anything: it is whatever the engineer decided to pay for.

In the Reward Arena the payment table is short. Every move costs `STEP_COST`, because a Kobuki base burns 12 W just standing still. Rolling onto the charging dock pays `DOCK_REWARD`. Rolling over the stair edge pays `HAZARD_REWARD` and the run is over, because the robot is now on the floor below.

The agent never reads that table. It sees the numbers arriving one at a time and nothing else. That is the whole distance from control: you do not tell it what to do, you tell it what you are willing to pay for. Which also means every mistake in the payment table comes back as a behaviour you never asked for.

Reward is a design decision, not a measurement.

lessons.title: One Turn of the Loop
lessons.goal: Run the agent and environment loop for a fixed policy and log every turn.
lessons.theory:
The loop has exactly four moving parts and never grows more. The agent reads a **state**, picks an **action**, the environment answers with a **reward** and the next state, and a flag says whether the episode is over.

In code that is two lines, and they are the two lines the rest of the course keeps rewriting. The policy turns a state into an action. The environment turns a state and an action into three things at once.

The arena in this lesson is a corridor of nine cells with the dock at cell 6. Think of a robot on a rail in a warehouse aisle: action 1 drives right, anything else drives left, and the walls at both ends do not move. The environment is written for you, closed, and the agent may not look inside it. That restriction is the whole point of the field: if you could look inside, you would plan instead of learn.

lessons.title: Two Ways a Run Can End
lessons.goal: Separate a terminal state from a step budget that ran out.
lessons.theory:
An episode ends for one of two reasons and they are not the same reason.

**Termination** is the environment saying there is nothing after this: the robot docked, or it went over the stair edge. **Truncation** is you saying you are out of patience: the step budget ran out while the world was still perfectly alive.

Mixing them up is a classic and expensive bug. A run that hit the clock is not a run that succeeded, and if your training code writes both down as done it will teach the agent that stalling near the wall is a fine way to finish. Later, when you bootstrap a value from the last state, a truncated episode still has a future and a terminated one does not.

So an honest episode runner reports which of the two happened, every time.

lessons.title: The Sum That Matters
lessons.goal: Score two policies by the return of an episode instead of by a single reward.
lessons.theory:
One reward tells you nothing. The dock pays 10 whether you reached it in eight steps or in eighty, and the step cost punishes you the same whether you were on your way somewhere or wandering.

The quantity that ranks behaviour is the **return**: the sum of every reward collected in the episode. Write it `G`. Comparing two policies means running each of them and comparing their returns, and it is the first honest measurement in the whole field.

It is also the first place where a number can lie to you. A return is one sample of one episode. On a deterministic corridor that is enough, and you will see it is not enough the moment the floor turns slippery.

lessons.title: It Optimises What You Paid For
lessons.goal: Measure a shaping bonus that pays a policy more for loitering than for docking.
lessons.theory:
The first thing engineers do when an agent will not learn is add a helpful bonus. The dock is far away and the reward is sparse, so they pay the robot a little for being **near** the dock, to point it in the right direction.

That bonus is a new term in the payment table, and the agent will collect it exactly as written. If standing next to the dock pays, then standing next to the dock forever pays forever, and docking ends the payments. You have not given it a hint. You have given it a better job than the one you wanted done.

This is not a rare failure. It is the default outcome of hand written shaping, and there is a form of shaping that provably cannot do it, which you will build much later. For now, measure the hole: run a policy that docks and a policy that loiters, once with the step cost switched off and once with it back on, and read the four numbers.

lessons.hint: With the step cost at zero the loiterer collects the bonus every second turn and never runs out of turns.

lessons.title: Cells and Bearings
lessons.goal: Turn a state and an action into the next cell of the arena grid.
lessons.theory:
The Reward Arena is a five by five patch of warehouse floor seen from the ceiling camera. A **state** is the cell the robot occupies, written as a `(row, column)` tuple with row 0 at the top. An **action** is one of four bearings, and `ACTIONS` holds their row and column offsets in the order north, east, south, west.

Discretising the floor into cells is a modelling decision with a price. A real Kobuki base does not teleport between tiles: it accelerates, drifts and stops, and the grid pretends none of that happens. In exchange you get 25 states instead of a continuous plane, which is what makes a table of values fit in memory and converge before the battery dies.

Every method in this course lives on top of that trade. Keep it in mind when the tables stop fitting.

lessons.title: The Wall Does Not Move
lessons.goal: Refuse moves into shelving and count how many bearings each cell has left.
lessons.theory:
Four shelving units stand in the arena at the cells listed in `WALLS`. They are not states: the robot can never be inside one, and a bearing that points into one is refused exactly like a bearing that points off the floor.

That detail matters more than it looks. A refused move still costs a step, so a wall is not neutral: it is a place where the agent pays and learns nothing. Agents that discover a wall early spend many episodes rediscovering that pushing it does nothing, and every one of those steps is real battery on a real robot.

Counting the bearings that actually lead somewhere gives you a first map of where the arena is tight. The cells with few open bearings are the ones a learner will take longest to get right.

lessons.title: A Policy Is a Table
lessons.goal: Store a deterministic policy as one action per state and run an episode from it.
lessons.theory:
A **policy** is the answer to the only question the robot ever asks: I am here, what do I do. When the arena has 21 reachable cells, the honest form of that answer is a table with 21 entries.

Writing it as a table instead of as a rule matters, because a table is what learning can change. A rule like go east then north is a program you wrote; a table is a set of numbers an algorithm can edit one cell at a time. Every method from chapter 4 onwards edits tables.

The policy in this lesson is a wall hugger: drive east along the bottom until the last column, then drive north up the edge. It never goes near the stair edge, which is why it survives, and it is the behaviour a learner will have to discover on its own by chapter 6.

lessons.title: The Same Chaos Twice
lessons.goal: Seed a private random stream so an experiment repeats exactly.
lessons.theory:
Reinforcement learning is built on sampling, and a result you cannot reproduce is not a result. Two rules keep this course honest.

First, **own your stream**. `random.Random(seed)` builds a generator that belongs to your function, and nothing else in the program can advance it. Calling the module level `random.random()` shares one stream with every library that ever touched it, so adding a print statement somewhere else can change your numbers.

Second, **do not iterate over a set**. A seeded stream fixes the dice, not the order you walk your states in, and set iteration order for tuples of small integers is an implementation detail, not a promise. Whenever you sweep states, sweep `sorted(...)` or a list you built yourself. This is the bug that survives a seed and looks exactly like a real result until it moves.

The lesson below runs the same experiment twice with one seed and once with another, and prints whether the counts match.
lessons.task: Finish `blind_walk(seed, episodes)` so it owns its stream with `rng = random.Random(seed)`, picks every bearing with `action = rng.randrange(len(ACTIONS))`, and returns how many episodes docked, fell and ran out of steps.
lessons.hint: Build the generator once per call, outside the episode loop, or every episode restarts the same dice.

lessons.goal: Compute the size of a tabular policy and the number of policies it could be.

Before you learn anything, count what you are about to learn. A tabular method stores one number per state and action, so the table has `len(cells) * len(ACTIONS)` entries and there is no way around that product.

That gap between a small table and an enormous policy space is the reason value based methods exist. They never enumerate policies. They improve one, using the table, one state at a time.

lessons.title: The Slippery Floor
lessons.goal: Add a slip probability to the transition and measure how often the bearing survives.
lessons.theory:
A deterministic grid is a lie you tell yourself for one chapter. Real wheels slip on dust, on cable covers, on the shiny strip where the floor paint changed, and the bearing that leaves the planner is not always the bearing the base executes.

Model it the cheap way: with probability `slip` the commanded bearing is replaced by one of the two perpendicular bearings, listed in `PERPENDICULAR`. Nothing else changes. The environment is still a grid, still 21 states, still four actions, but the transition is now a distribution instead of a function.

Everything downstream inherits that. A value is now an expectation, a single episode return stops being evidence, and a policy that hugs the stair edge because it is one cell shorter becomes a policy that eventually falls off it.

lessons.title: One Interface, Any Arena
lessons.goal: Wrap the arena in a reset and step object so later algorithms never touch its internals.
lessons.theory:
From here on the learning code should not know what an arena is. It resets, it steps, it reads three values back. That is the contract every simulator and every real robot driver in this field exposes, and keeping to it is what lets you swap a grid for a Gazebo model or for a real base without touching the learner.

The object holds two pieces of state: where the robot is and how many turns it has spent. The turn counter belongs to the environment, not to the algorithm, because the algorithm has no business enforcing your time budget and will forget to.

When the interface is clean, the honesty problem of this course gets easier to see: the learner cannot tell whether it is stepping a simulator or a real machine, and it will happily spend a million steps either way.

lessons.hint: The class holds state, the free functions hold rules. Do not re implement the rules inside the class.

lessons.title: The Log of a Life

Every algorithm after chapter 4 learns from the same five field record: the state, the action, the reward, the next state and the done flag. Store anything less and you will be re running episodes to recover it.

A log like this is also what turns a robot session into an asset. Twenty minutes of teleoperated driving becomes a file you can learn from a thousand times, which is the only reason anything ever gets trained on hardware.

lessons.title: The Discount Is a Choice
lessons.goal: Compute the discounted return of an episode for several discount factors.
lessons.theory:
The plain return adds every reward with equal weight, which says a charge in ten minutes is worth exactly as much as a charge now. No engineer believes that, and no battery does either.

The **discount factor** `gamma` fixes it by multiplying the reward at step `t` by `gamma ** t`. With gamma at 1.0 nothing is discounted. With gamma at 0.5 a reward eight steps out is worth less than half a percent of the same reward now.

Gamma is not a property of the robot and not something you measure. It is a knob that says how far ahead this machine should care, and it silently rewrites which behaviour is optimal. Two engineers with the same arena and different gammas get different policies and both are correct.

The rest of this chapter is about reading that knob honestly.

That identity is not a trick for speed. It is the same shape as the Bellman equation you will meet in chapter 3, and it is worth recognising it here where there is no value table and nothing to be confused about: a return is a reward plus a discounted continuation.

This lesson counts multiplications so the saving is a number and not a claim. The forward version pays a full power at every step, the reverse version pays one.

lessons.title: The Horizon in Steps
lessons.goal: Convert a discount factor into the number of steps the agent effectively sees.
lessons.theory:
Gamma is a number between 0 and 1 and it is useless as an intuition. Convert it into steps and it becomes a design parameter you can argue about.

The standard conversion is the **effective horizon**, `1 / (1 - gamma)`. It is the point where the discount has eaten a reward down to about 37 percent of its face value, and it is close enough to a planning distance to be worth quoting. Gamma 0.9 sees about ten steps. Gamma 0.99 sees about a hundred.

Now put units on it. If the base takes 0.4 seconds per cell, gamma 0.9 is a robot that cares about the next four seconds and is genuinely blind to anything past it. If the dock is thirty steps away, that robot will never learn to go there, no matter how long you train it, and the fault is in the knob and not in the algorithm.

lessons.title: Why Not Gamma One
lessons.goal: Show that an undiscounted continuing task has no finite return and a discounted one does.
lessons.theory:
Episodes end, so gamma 1.0 is legal there. A **continuing** task never ends: a patrol robot that circles a warehouse aisle forever, paying its step cost every turn. Add up that stream with gamma 1.0 and the answer is minus infinity, which ranks every possible policy equally badly.

With gamma below 1 the same infinite stream has a finite value, and there is a closed form for the constant case: `PER_STEP / (1.0 - gamma)`. That number is what a value table would eventually hold, and it is why discounting is not only about patience. It is what makes the maths defined at all.

The average reward formulation is the other way out of this, and it is the right one for genuinely endless jobs. It is also harder and outside this course.

lessons.title: How Far It Will Walk
lessons.goal: Find the maximum distance a discount factor is willing to travel for a fixed payout.
lessons.theory:
Here is the version of gamma you can put in a design review. Given a payout at the end and a step cost along the way, there is a distance beyond which the discounted return of walking there goes negative, and past that distance the agent prefers to do nothing.

Solve it by walking outwards: extend the route one cell at a time and stop when the return stops being worth it. The number that comes out is a **reach**, in cells, and it can be compared directly against your floor plan.

This is also the cheapest sanity check in the field. Measure the distance from the worst starting cell to the dock, compute the reach for your gamma, and if the reach is smaller you can stop tuning: no amount of training fixes a horizon that does not span the job.

Then read the reach of each discount factor against the eight cells the arena needs.

lessons.title: Return Is Not Reward
lessons.goal: Compute the return remaining at every step of an episode and compare it to the reward there.
lessons.theory:
The reward at a step and the return from a step are different quantities and confusing them produces value tables that look plausible and are wrong.

The reward is what that one transition paid. The **return from step t** is what the rest of the episode paid, discounted back to `t`. In the arena the reward is -1 for almost every step of a successful run, while the return climbs steadily as the dock gets closer. The reward is flat and the return has a shape, and the shape is the information.

Computing it is the reverse scan again, but stored per step instead of collapsed: the return at `t` is the reward at `t` plus gamma times the return at `t + 1`. Those numbers are exactly what a Monte Carlo learner will average in chapter 5, so get them right here.
lessons.task: Finish the reverse scan so that `for t in reversed(range(len(rewards) - 1))` it fills in each entry with `returns[t] = rewards[t] + gamma * returns[t + 1]`. The last entry is already set, since after it there is nothing.
lessons.hint: Print the two columns side by side: the reward stays flat while the return climbs towards the dock.

    returns[-1] = rewards[-1]
    # TODO: fill the rest backwards

    returns = [0.0] * len(rewards)
    returns[-1] = rewards[-1]
    for t in reversed(range(len(rewards) - 1)):

lessons.title: The Average of Many Lives
lessons.goal: Estimate an expected return by sampling and watch the estimate settle as episodes pile up.
lessons.theory:
On a slippery floor a single return is a coin flip, so the quantity that means anything is the **expected** return, the average over the distribution of episodes the policy produces.

You cannot compute that expectation without a model, but you can sample it, and the error of a sample mean shrinks with the square root of the number of episodes. Square root is slow: four times the episodes buys about half the error, which is the arithmetic behind every complaint about how much data this field needs.

One batch cannot show you its own error, so the run below repeats the whole estimate on 24 independent seeds and prints the spread between them. That spread is the honest error bar, and watching it fall from about 0.8 to under 0.1 costs 64 times the episodes.
lessons.task: Finish `expected_return(seed, episodes)` so it accumulates every sampled episode with `total = total + episode_return(rng)` and reports the average as `mean = total / episodes`. Then read the spread column across the four batch sizes.
lessons.hint: One stream for the whole batch. Rebuilding the generator inside the episode loop would sample the same episode over and over.

import random
import statistics

SLIP = 0.25
SEEDS = 24

def episode_return(rng, gamma=0.95, max_steps=40):
    cell = 0
    g = 0.0
    weight = 1.0
    for _ in range(max_steps):
        forward = rng.random() > SLIP
        cell = cell + 1 if forward else max(cell - 1, 0)
        if cell >= 8:
            g = g + weight * 10.0
            break
        g = g + weight * -1.0
        weight = weight * gamma
    return g

def expected_return(seed, episodes):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    total = 0.0
    mean = 0.0
    for _ in range(episodes):
        total = total + episode_return(rng)
    mean = total / episodes
    return mean

for episodes in (20, 80, 320, 1280):
    batch = [expected_return(100 + s, episodes) for s in range(SEEDS)]
    print("episodes", episodes, "estimate", round(statistics.mean(batch), 4),
          "spread", round(statistics.pstdev(batch), 4))

lessons.title: The Discounted Damage
lessons.goal: Measure how much of a distant hazard penalty survives the discount.
lessons.theory:
The discount does not only fade rewards. It fades **penalties**, and that is the version nobody puts on the slide.

A stair edge that costs -20 when you touch it costs `gamma ** distance` times -20 when it is that many cells away. At gamma 0.9 a hazard ten steps out is worth about -7, and at twenty steps it is under -3, which is less than the cost of three wasted moves. A policy optimising that number will happily route past the stairs to save a couple of cells.

So the horizon is a safety parameter, not only a performance one. When the consequence is a broken robot rather than a slower one, the discount is the wrong tool to express it, and you want a hard constraint or a shield instead. Chapter 8 builds one and measures what it saves.

lessons.hint: Compare each row against `DETOUR_COST`, the price of the three extra cells a safe route would need.

DETOUR_COST = -3.0

    weight = 0.0
    seen = 0.0
    # TODO: fade the penalty by the distance and report what is left
    return weight, seen

for gamma in (0.9, 0.99):
    for distance in (1, 5, 10, 20):
        weight, seen = seen_penalty(distance, gamma)
        print("gamma", gamma, "distance", distance, "weight", round(weight, 4),

DETOUR_COST = -3.0

    weight = gamma ** distance
    seen = weight * HAZARD_REWARD
    return weight, seen

lessons.title: The Value of Standing Here
lessons.goal: Estimate the value of a state under a policy by averaging sampled returns.
lessons.theory:
The **value** of a state under a policy is the expected return if you drop the robot there and let the policy run. Written `V(s)`, it is one number per cell and it is the object every method in this course is trying to get right.

On a floor that slips, that expectation is not something you can read off a single run, so the first way to get it is brute force: drop the robot on the cell many times, average the returns. That works, needs no model at all, and it is exactly what a Monte Carlo learner does in chapter 5.

It is also slow enough to be worth measuring. Each sample is a full episode, and a real robot cannot be teleported to an arbitrary cell to start one, which is the first crack in the idea that a robot can learn this way on hardware.
lessons.task: Finish `value_of(cell, policy, rng, episodes)` so it averages sampled returns: accumulate with `total = total + rollout(cell, policy, rng)` and finish with `return total / episodes`. Read the values it prints for three starting cells.
lessons.hint: One stream, passed in from outside, so the three cells do not all replay the same dice.

lessons.title: The Bellman Promise
lessons.goal: Measure how badly a value table breaks the one step consistency condition.
lessons.theory:
Sampling is not the only way to know a value. A correct table obeys a local promise at every state: the value here equals the reward for the step the policy takes plus gamma times the value of where it lands. Terminal states end the chain, so their continuation is zero and not the value of the cell the robot is lying on.

The amount by which a table breaks that promise is the **Bellman residual**. It is a per state number and its maximum over the arena is a complete health check: zero everywhere means the table is exactly right, and nothing else does.

This is the tool that tells you whether your evaluation converged, and later whether your learner is still learning. It costs one sweep and it is the first thing to print when a value table looks wrong.
lessons.task: Finish `residuals(v, policy, gamma)`. For each non terminal cell build `target = r + gamma * (0.0 if done else v[nxt])`, take `residual = abs(v[s] - target)` and keep the largest. Compare the zero table against the converged one.
lessons.hint: A terminal cell has no step to take, so it contributes no residual at all.

value: target = r + gamma * (0.0 if done else v[nxt])

lessons.title: Sweeping the Board
lessons.goal: Run one sweep of iterative policy evaluation and report the largest change.
lessons.theory:
Iterative policy evaluation fixes the residual the blunt way: visit every state, overwrite its value with the one step target, repeat. Each pass is a **sweep**, and the largest change in a sweep is the number that tells you whether another one is worth running.

One detail decides whether this is reproducible: the order you visit the states in. Seeding the random generator does not help here, because there is no randomness. What bites is iterating over a `set`, whose order for tuples is an implementation detail that can differ between runs. Sweep a list you built yourself, or a `sorted` view of your keys, always.

That is not a style preference. An in place sweep uses values updated earlier in the same pass, so a different order gives different intermediate numbers, and a lesson whose printed delta moves between runs cannot be taught.
lessons.task: Finish `sweep(v, policy, gamma)` so each non terminal cell is overwritten with `v[s] = r + gamma * (0.0 if done else v[nxt])` and the pass reports its biggest movement with `delta = max(delta, abs(v[s] - before))`. Read the first four deltas.
lessons.hint: Save the old value before you overwrite it, because the change is measured against the value that was there.

value: v[s] = r + gamma * (0.0 if done else v[nxt])

lessons.title: Until It Stops Moving
lessons.goal: Iterate policy evaluation to a threshold and report the sweeps it needed.
lessons.theory:
Sweeping once is not evaluation. Evaluation is sweeping until the table stops moving, and the stopping rule is a threshold on the largest change.

The threshold is a real decision, not a formality. Set it at 0.1 and the table is still visibly wrong near the dock; set it at 1e-12 and you spend sweeps buying digits nobody reads. A useful default is a value small compared to the smallest reward difference you care about, which here is the one step cost.

Also count the sweeps. That count is the cost of evaluation, it grows with the horizon rather than with the number of states, and it is the number that decides whether a planner is fast enough to run between two camera frames.
lessons.task: Finish `evaluate(policy, gamma)` so it counts each pass with `sweeps = sweeps + 1` and stops early when `if delta < THRESHOLD:`. Compare how many sweeps two discount factors need.
lessons.hint: The loop body is the sweep you already wrote. All that is new is the counter and the exit.

lessons.title: In Place or in Copy
lessons.goal: Compare a sweep that reads its own updates against one that reads last sweep only.
lessons.theory:
There are two honest ways to run a sweep. **Jacobi** builds a fresh table from the old one, so every state in the pass sees the same snapshot. **Gauss-Seidel** writes into the table it is reading, so a state updated early in the pass helps the states updated after it.

Gauss-Seidel usually converges in fewer sweeps and costs no extra memory. The arena shows why: value flows backwards from the dock, so a pass that happens to run in that direction carries information several cells at once instead of one cell per sweep.

The price is that the answer now depends on the visiting order, which is why the previous lesson was so insistent about fixing it. The run below counts three configurations on a policy that climbs towards the dock: Jacobi, Gauss-Seidel in the order `cells()` returns, and Gauss-Seidel reversed. Two of them are the same algorithm with the list turned around, and they do not cost the same.
lessons.task: Finish the Jacobi sweep so it works on a snapshot: take `fresh = dict(v)` at the top, write every new value into that copy with `fresh[s] = r + gamma * (0.0 if done else v[nxt])`, and return the copy. Then read the three sweep counts.
lessons.hint: The Gauss-Seidel version is already written below, and the only difference is which table the right hand side reads.

value: fresh[s] = r + gamma * (0.0 if done else v[nxt])

lessons.title: The Value of a Bad Policy
lessons.goal: Evaluate two policies on the same arena and read the gap at the start cell.
lessons.theory:
Evaluation does not judge. It answers what a policy is worth, and a policy that drives into the stair edge gets an honest number for doing so.

The wall hugger goes east along the bottom and north up the last column, eight steps, no danger. The shortcut climbs north to the middle row and then drives east, which is a cell shorter on paper and ends in the hazard. Their values at the start cell differ by more than twenty, and no amount of tuning turns the second into the first: the fault is in the policy, not in the evaluation.

This is the pattern that makes value based control work. Score policies with the same machinery, then change the policy where the score says it is losing. Chapter 4 automates exactly that.
lessons.task: Evaluate both stored policies with the `evaluate` function and print the gap at the start. Put the safe one in `safe = evaluate(HUGGER, GAMMA)` and the other in `risky`, then report `gap = safe[START] - risky[START]`.
lessons.hint: Both policies are already tables. Nothing about the evaluation changes between them.

lessons.title: Where the Table Says Danger
lessons.goal: Print a value table as a grid and locate the worst cell on it.
lessons.theory:
A value table is 21 numbers, and 21 numbers in a column teach nothing. Printed on the floor plan they become a map, and the map is readable at a glance: values climb towards the dock and collapse around whatever the policy walks into.

Under the shortcut policy the collapse is around the stair edge, and it is not one cell. Every cell whose policy leads towards the hazard inherits a discounted share of the penalty, so the damage spreads outwards along the path, fading by gamma per cell. That spread is the value function doing its job: it is telling you which parts of the floor this policy has ruined.

Printing this grid is the debugging tool of the whole course. When a learner misbehaves later, print its table on the floor plan before you touch a hyperparameter.
lessons.task: Finish the grid printer so a wall prints as the fixed marker and any other cell prints its value with `row.append('%7.2f' % v[(r, c)])`. Then find the lowest valued reachable cell with `worst = min(inner, key=lambda c: v[c])`.
lessons.hint: `inner` already holds the non terminal cells, so the worst cell will not come back as the stair edge itself.

lessons.title: Expectation Over a Slippery Floor
lessons.goal: Evaluate a policy under stochastic transitions by weighting every outcome.
lessons.theory:
When the floor slips, the one step target stops being a single number. The commanded bearing survives with probability `1 - slip` and each perpendicular bearing takes over with half the rest, so the value of a state is the **weighted average** over those three landings.

Nothing else about evaluation changes. The sweep is the same, the threshold is the same, only the target is now a sum over outcomes. That is the general form, and the deterministic version you wrote earlier is the case where one outcome has probability one.

The result is worth reading carefully. The wall hugger loses a little value everywhere, because slipping costs steps, and it loses a lot in the cells where a slip points at the stair edge. A policy that was safe on paper is only mostly safe on a floor with dust on it.
lessons.task: Finish `expected_target(s, action, v, gamma, slip)` so it walks the outcome list with `for executed, prob in outcomes(action, slip):` and accumulates `total = total + prob * (r + gamma * (0.0 if done else v[nxt]))`. Compare the dry and slippery values.
lessons.hint: `outcomes` already returns the three pairs and their probabilities add up to one, so no extra normalisation is needed.

value: for executed, prob in outcomes(action, slip):
total = total + prob * (r + gamma * (0.0 if done else v[nxt]))

lessons.title: The Residual Tells You When to Stop
lessons.goal: Compare the theoretical error bound of a stopping rule against the error it actually left.
lessons.theory:
A threshold on the largest change is not an error. What you want to know is how far the table is from the truth, and there is a bound for it: if the last sweep moved nothing by more than `delta`, then no entry is further from the truth than `gamma * delta / (1 - gamma)`.

Read that factor before you trust a stopping rule. At gamma 0.99 it multiplies your threshold by 99, so stopping at 1.0 admits an error near 100, which on this arena is larger than every value in the table.

This arena also happens to contain the exact worst case the bound was derived from. The cell at `(1, 0)` faces a shelving unit, the wall hugger tells it to drive east, and it stays where it is, so its value obeys a pure geometric recursion at rate gamma and it converges no faster than the bound allows. That is why the two columns below come out equal to the digit: the bound is not pessimistic here, it is attained. Watch the sweep count instead to see what tightening the threshold actually buys.
lessons.task: Finish the comparison: compute `bound = gamma * delta / (1.0 - gamma)` from the last sweep, and measure the truth with `actual = max(abs(v[s] - exact[s]) for s in cells())`. Check that the bound holds for all four thresholds and read the sweeps each one cost.
lessons.hint: `exact` is the table evaluated to machine precision, so treat it as the truth for this measurement.

value: actual = max(abs(v[s] - exact[s]) for s in cells())

lessons.title: The Value of a Move
lessons.goal: Build the action value of every bearing from a state value table.
lessons.theory:
A value table tells you what a cell is worth and says nothing about what to do there. To act you need one number per **state and action**, and that is the action value `Q(s, a)`: the worth of taking that bearing here and then following the policy afterwards.

With a model you get it in one line of lookahead. Take the step, collect the reward, add the discounted value of where you landed. Four bearings, four numbers, and the best of them is the best thing to do in that cell.

That is the whole reason Q exists. A state value needs a model to be turned into a decision; an action value is already a decision. Chapter 6 will learn Q directly from experience precisely because the model is the part a robot does not have.
lessons.task: Finish `q_values(s, v, gamma)` so it loops with `for a in range(len(ACTIONS))` and appends the lookahead score `q = r + gamma * (0.0 if done else v[nxt])` for each bearing. Read the four numbers it prints for three cells.
lessons.hint: A step that ends the episode has no continuation, so its score is the reward and nothing else.

value: q = r + gamma * (0.0 if done else v[nxt])

lessons.title: The Greedy Reading
lessons.goal: Extract a policy from action values with a tie break that never changes between runs.
lessons.theory:
Reading a policy out of action values is one `max` per state, and it is also the place where a reinforcement learning course most often stops being reproducible.

At the start of training every bearing scores the same, so **every state is a tie**. If you break those ties at random, or by iterating a set, the printed policy changes between runs and so does everything downstream of it. `max(range(len(ACTIONS)), key=...)` keeps the first best index, which is a rule, deterministic and boring, and boring is what you want.

There is one honest use for random tie breaking: it stops a fresh agent from marching north forever because north happens to be index zero. That is an exploration problem and chapter 6 solves it with an explicit exploration rule instead, which you can seed, log and switch off.
lessons.task: Finish `greedy_from(v, gamma)` so each cell picks `best = max(range(len(ACTIONS)), key=lambda a: scores[a])` and stores it with `greedy[s] = best`. The run prints the policy twice and checks the two readings are identical.
lessons.hint: `max` keeps the first of several equal keys, so a four way tie always reads as bearing 0.

lessons.title: Better by One Step
lessons.goal: Show that acting greedily with respect to a policy value never makes any state worse.
lessons.theory:
The policy improvement theorem is the load bearing result of this chapter, and it is short. Take any policy, compute its values, then in every state act greedily with respect to those values. The new policy is at least as good **in every state**, and strictly better somewhere unless the old one was already optimal.

That is a very strong promise from a very cheap operation. You do not need to search policies, you do not need to try things: one evaluation and one greedy pass, and you have provably climbed.

Measure it rather than believing it. The run below evaluates the wall hugger, builds the greedy policy from its values, evaluates that, and counts the cells where the value went up, went down, or stayed. The count of cells that got worse is the interesting one, and it should be zero.

lessons.hint: `argmax_action` already scores the four bearings against the table you pass it, so improvement is one dictionary comprehension.

value: improved = {s: argmax_action(s, before, GAMMA) for s in INNER}
better = sum(1 for s in INNER if after[s] > before[s] + 1e-9)

lessons.title: The Two Step Dance
lessons.goal: Alternate evaluation and improvement until the policy stops changing.
lessons.theory:
Policy iteration is the previous lesson in a loop. Evaluate, improve, repeat, and stop when improving changes nothing.

It terminates and it terminates fast. There are finitely many deterministic policies, every round is strictly better than the last, so the loop cannot cycle, and in practice it lands in a handful of rounds even when the policy space has trillions of members. The arena has 4 to the power of 21 policies and this loop will visit about four of them.

The stopping test is exact equality of two tables, not a threshold. That works because the policy is discrete, and it is one of the few places in this field where you get to compare for equality and mean it.
lessons.task: Finish the loop. Each round build the greedy table, stop when `if improved == policy:` because nothing moved, and otherwise carry on with `policy = improved`. Report the rounds and the final value at the start.
lessons.hint: Start from any policy at all. The hugger is a reasonable one and a table of zeros would also work.

lessons.title: Skip the Middle Man
lessons.goal: Solve the arena with value iteration and read the optimal policy off the result.
lessons.theory:
Policy iteration evaluates a policy to convergence and only then improves it, which is a lot of sweeps spent perfecting the value of a policy you are about to throw away.

**Value iteration** cuts that short. Instead of the value of the current policy, each sweep writes the best one step target: the maximum over bearings. There is no explicit policy inside the loop at all, and the policy is read off once at the end. It is the Bellman optimality equation used as an assignment.

This is the algorithm to reach for when you have a model and a modest state space, and it is what the project chapter uses to produce the ground truth that the learner will be graded against.
lessons.task: Finish `value_iteration(gamma)` so each cell takes the best available target with `v[s] = max(q_values(s, v, gamma))`, and once the sweeps are done read the answer with `policy = {s: argmax_action(s, v, gamma) for s in INNER}`.
lessons.hint: The sweep is the one from chapter 3 with the policy lookup replaced by a maximum.

lessons.title: The Same Answer, Two Roads
lessons.goal: Check that policy iteration and value iteration agree, and compare what each cost.
lessons.theory:
Two algorithms that solve the same equation should produce the same policy, and if yours do not, one of them has a bug. Checking that is a five line experiment and it is worth doing every time you write a planner.

Agreement on the **policy** is the right test, not agreement on the values. Values can differ in the last digits because the two loops stop on different criteria, while the bearings they imply are identical. Comparing the wrong one of those two things sends people hunting for bugs that are not there.

The costs are what differ. Policy iteration runs few rounds and each round is a full evaluation; value iteration runs many cheap sweeps. The totals below are within a factor of a few, and on larger problems the balance moves.

lessons.hint: Compare bearings, not values, since the two loops stop on different rules and their last digits will not match.

value: agree = sum(1 for s in INNER if pi_policy[s] == vi_policy[s])

lessons.title: Reading the Arrows
lessons.goal: Draw a policy on the floor plan and walk it to check where it ends.
lessons.theory:
A policy printed as 21 integers is unreadable. Printed as arrows on the floor plan it is inspectable in a second, and reviewing it that way catches the class of bug no metric catches: an optimal looking value table whose arrows point somewhere absurd in one corner.

Draw it, then walk it. The arrows tell you what the policy intends, and walking from the start tells you what it does, which are different claims. A policy can look sensible cell by cell and still contain a two cell cycle that no arrow reveals on its own.

So this lesson prints both: the map, and the path the robot takes when it obeys the map. On the optimal policy that path is eight cells long and it does not go near the middle of the arena.
