lessons.hint: The bearing order is north, east, south, west, the same order the offsets are listed in.

lessons.title: The Model You Do Not Have
lessons.goal: Count the environment queries a planner makes and price them as real robot moves.
lessons.theory:
Everything in this chapter called `step`. That call is the **model**: given a state and a bearing it returns the landing, the reward and the flag, instantly, for any cell, including cells the robot has never visited and cells beyond the stair edge.

A real robot has no such function. To find out what happens when you drive east from the tile next to the stairs, you drive east from the tile next to the stairs. Every model query a planner makes for free is, on hardware, a physical move that costs time and sometimes the robot.

So count them. Instrument the model, run value iteration, and price the queries at the 0.4 seconds the base takes to cross a cell. The number that comes out is the reason the rest of this course is about learning without a model, and chapter 8 is about what that costs instead.
lessons.task: Count the queries. Bump the counter inside the wrapper with `MODEL_CALLS[0] = MODEL_CALLS[0] + 1`, and after the planner has finished read it back with `queries = MODEL_CALLS[0]`. Then read the hours those queries would have cost on hardware.
lessons.hint: The wrapper has to be the only way the planner reaches the environment, so count inside it and not at the call sites.

lessons.title: Optimal Return, Measured
lessons.goal: Confirm that the value at the start equals the discounted return the policy actually collects.
lessons.theory:
A value is a promise about a return. On a deterministic arena that promise is checkable to the last digit: run the policy from the start, discount every reward by how late it arrived, and the total must equal the table entry for the start cell.

Doing this once, by hand, is worth more than any amount of trust in the algorithm. It closes the loop between the abstraction and the robot, and it catches the two classic sign errors: discounting the first reward, and adding the terminal value on top of the terminal reward.

The same check applied to the wall hugger shows the gap the planner bought, which is the number a project review actually asks for.
lessons.task: Walk each policy and accumulate its discounted return with `realised = realised + weight * r`. Then confirm the promise with `match = abs(realised - v[START]) < 1e-9` for the optimal policy.
lessons.hint: The first reward is undiscounted, so multiply the weight by gamma after using it, not before.

lessons.title: No Map, Only Footsteps
lessons.goal: Collect episodes without a model and measure how much of the arena they cover.
lessons.theory:
From here the model is gone. There is no `step` you may call on a hypothetical cell, only a robot that is somewhere, does something, and reports what happened. Everything the learner knows has to arrive through that stream.

The first consequence is coverage. A planner touched every state and every bearing because it could ask; a learner only knows the cells it has stood on. States the policy avoids stay unknown forever, which sounds fine until you notice that the states it avoids are exactly the ones you need values for in order to know whether avoiding them was right.

The policy used here is the table chapter 4 planned on the dry model, running now on a floor that slips one time in ten. The episodes start from a cell drawn at random, which is a convenience a simulator has and a robot does not: on hardware every episode starts wherever the last one ended.
lessons.task: Finish `collect(policy, rng, count)` so it records each transition with `trace.append((cell, a, r, nxt, done))`, keeps a coverage set with `seen.add(cell)`, and returns the episodes together with how many distinct cells were touched.
lessons.hint: Coverage is about the cells the robot stood on, so add the cell before the step, not the one it landed on.

lessons.title: The Average of Returns
lessons.goal: Estimate state values by averaging the returns that followed each visit.
lessons.theory:
Monte Carlo prediction is the definition of value turned into code. The value of a state is the expected return from it, so wait until the episode is over, compute the return that actually followed each visit, and average.

No model, no bootstrapping, no assumptions. The estimate is unbiased from the first sample, and its error is pure sampling noise that shrinks with the square root of the visits. Its weakness is the waiting: nothing is learned until the episode ends, and on a task that can run for ten minutes that is ten minutes per data point.

The run compares the averages against the exact values computed with the slip model, which the learner is not allowed to see. That comparison is the only way to know an estimator works, and it is a luxury you have exactly once, on a toy arena, before every real problem takes it away.
lessons.task: Finish the Monte Carlo pass. Walk each episode backwards accumulating `g = r + GAMMA * g`, then for every visited cell bank the sample with `totals[s] = totals[s] + g` and `counts[s] = counts[s] + 1`.
lessons.hint: The trace stores the reward of each transition, so the return for the visit at index `t` is built from the tail of the list.

lessons.title: Every Visit Counts
lessons.goal: Compare first visit and every visit Monte Carlo on the same episodes.
lessons.theory:
An episode can pass through the same cell twice, which happens constantly on a slippery floor. That leaves a choice: average the return from **every** visit, or only from the **first** visit in each episode.

Every visit is simpler and its samples are correlated, because two visits in one episode share most of their future. First visit throws data away and buys independence for what is left. Both converge to the same value and they disagree on the way there, which is the whole reason the distinction has a name.

Run them on the identical episode set, so the difference you see is the estimator and not the dice. On this arena the gap is small and it is not zero, and if you ever see it come out exactly zero, your episodes never revisited a cell and the experiment did not test anything.
lessons.task: Finish the first visit variant: skip a repeat with `if s in seen_here:` and otherwise remember it with `seen_here.add(s)` before banking the sample. The every visit version is already written.
lessons.hint: Walking the trace backwards means the last occurrence is met first, so build the set of visited cells from a forward pass or from the indices.

lessons.title: The Running Mean
lessons.goal: Replace stored sums with an incremental update and prove the two agree.
lessons.theory:
Keeping a total and a count per state works and it does not scale. Every learner from here on updates a single number in place, and the identity that lets you do it is the **incremental mean**.

With `n` samples seen, the new average is the old average plus the new sample minus the old average, divided by `n`. Written as a step towards the sample it is `v = v + (g - v) / n`, and the shape of that line is the shape of every learning rule in the rest of this course: current estimate, plus a fraction of the error between it and something new.

Recognise the pattern now. Monte Carlo, TD, Q-learning and SARSA are the same line with different definitions of the target, and the fraction out front is the only thing you will end up tuning.
lessons.task: Finish the incremental version: count the sample with `n[s] = n[s] + 1` and move the estimate with `v[s] = v[s] + (g - v[s]) / n[s]`. The batch version is already written, and the run checks that the two agree to machine precision.
lessons.hint: Increment the count before you divide by it, or the first sample divides by zero.

lessons.title: A Fixed Step Forgets
lessons.goal: Track a value that moves, and show why a constant learning rate beats an exact average.
lessons.theory:
Dividing by the sample count is the right thing to do when the truth stands still. It weights the first episode as heavily as the ten thousandth, so after enough data the estimate stops responding to anything.

Robots do not stand still. The dock contact resistance rises, a wheel wears, someone moves a shelf, and the value of a cell is now a different number than it was this morning. Replacing `1/n` with a constant `alpha` turns the average into an exponential window: recent samples dominate, old ones fade, and the estimate can follow.

The price is that it never settles, it hovers with a variance proportional to alpha. That trade is the entire tuning story of the learning rate, and this run makes it visible by moving the dock payout halfway through and measuring which estimator noticed.
lessons.task: Finish the constant rate learner so it steps towards each sample with `v[s] = v[s] + alpha * (g - v[s])`. Then read how far each estimator ends from the new truth in `error = abs(v[START] - truth)`.
lessons.hint: The payout changes at the halfway episode, so only the second half of the data describes the world the robot is in now.

lessons.title: Learn Before the End
lessons.goal: Update a value from a single transition using the estimate of the next state.
lessons.theory:
Monte Carlo waits for the episode to finish. **Temporal difference** learning does not: it updates from one transition, using its own estimate of the next state in place of the return it has not seen yet.

The target becomes the reward plus gamma times the value of where the robot landed, and the difference between that target and the current estimate is the **TD error**. It is the same line as the running mean with a different target, and that substitution is the single most important idea in the field.

It also means the learner is chasing a moving target built from its own guesses, which is called bootstrapping and is why TD can be biased early. In exchange it learns during the episode, works on tasks that never end, and needs no memory of the trajectory. Every practical algorithm here descends from it.
lessons.task: Finish the TD(0) update so each transition moves the estimate with `v[s] = v[s] + ALPHA * (r + GAMMA * (0.0 if done else v[nxt]) - v[s])`, walking the trace forwards with `for s, a, r, nxt, done in trace:`.
lessons.hint: A terminal landing has no value to bootstrap from, so its continuation is zero and not `v[nxt]`.

value: for s, a, r, nxt, done in trace:
v[s] = v[s] + ALPHA * (r + GAMMA * (0.0 if done else v[nxt]) - v[s])

lessons.title: The Error That Teaches
lessons.goal: Log the size of the TD error over training and show it shrinking.
lessons.theory:
The TD error is not only the thing that drives the update, it is the best progress signal a model free learner has. Big errors mean the table still disagrees with its own experience; small errors mean it has settled, right or wrong.

Watch it rather than the values. A value curve tells you a number moved, the mean absolute TD error tells you whether the learner is still learning, and it is the quantity to plot when someone asks whether training has converged.

Expect it to fall fast and then stop falling. With a constant learning rate the estimate never stops hopping around its target, so the curve flattens onto a floor set by alpha rather than heading to zero. That floor is not a bug and it is not convergence either.

And be careful with what a small error does not say. It means the table is self consistent, not correct: a learner that never visits a corner of the arena has no error there and no value either. Consistency and coverage are separate problems and you need both.
lessons.task: Log the errors. Compute the difference with `td = r + GAMMA * (0.0 if done else v[nxt]) - v[s]`, apply it, and record its size with `sizes.append(abs(td))`. Then read where the curve flattens.
lessons.hint: Record the error you used for the update, before the update changes the table.

value: td = r + GAMMA * (0.0 if done else v[nxt]) - v[s]

lessons.title: Bias Against Variance
lessons.goal: Compare Monte Carlo and TD on identical budgets and read where each one loses.
lessons.theory:
Monte Carlo is unbiased and noisy. Its target is a real return, so it is right on average from the first sample, and one unlucky slip near the stairs drags a whole episode of estimates with it.

TD is biased and quiet. Its target leans on the table it is building, so while that table is wrong the target is wrong in a consistent direction. Its updates are small and correlated, and its spread between runs is much smaller.

One run cannot show either property, because one number contains the bias and the noise added together. So repeat both estimators on 12 seeds and split the error into its two halves: the **mean** error is the bias, the **spread** across seeds is the variance. The table below prints all four numbers. The Monte Carlo bias heads to zero and its spread only falls with the square root of the budget. The TD bias is a transient that grows while the table is still filling itself in and then decays, and at both ends of the run its spread is the smaller of the two.
lessons.task: Split the error. Collect the signed error at the start cell for each seed, then report `mc_bias = statistics.mean(mc_errors)` against the spread `td_spread = statistics.pstdev(td_errors)` and their two partners, and read which estimator is quieter.
lessons.hint: Signed errors, not absolute ones. Taking the absolute value first destroys exactly the cancellation that makes an unbiased estimator look unbiased.

lessons.title: Bootstrapping on a Lie
lessons.goal: Measure how long TD takes to recover from a badly initialised table.
lessons.theory:
TD builds its target out of the table it is writing, so whatever you put in that table at the start is an assertion the learner initially believes. Initialise every cell at 50 and the learner spends its first thousand episodes arguing itself out of a fantasy.

It does recover. The rewards are real and they arrive at every step, so the fantasy is contradicted from the terminal states backwards, one bootstrapped layer at a time. What it costs is episodes, and this lesson counts them.

The practical rule falls out of the measurement. Initialise near zero when you want fast, honest prediction. Initialise high on purpose when you want the agent to go and look at everything, which is a control trick called optimistic initialisation and it arrives in the next chapter. Same knob, opposite intent.
lessons.task: Finish the experiment: start every entry with `v = {c: start_value for c in INNER}`, run TD, and stop the moment `if worst_error(v, exact) < TOLERANCE:` holds. Report the episodes each starting point needed.
lessons.hint: Check the error once per episode, not once per transition, or the count you report is not in episodes.

value: v = {c: start_value for c in INNER}

lessons.title: The Table of Moves
lessons.goal: Allocate an action value table and read a policy out of it.
lessons.theory:
Control needs one number per state **and bearing**, not one per state. That table is `Q`, it has `len(INNER) * len(ACTIONS)` entries, and unlike a value table it can be turned into behaviour without a model: look up the row, take the largest entry, drive.

Store it as a dictionary from cell to a list of four floats. The list index is the bearing, in the same north, east, south, west order the offsets use, and keeping that order consistent everywhere is worth more than it sounds: a transposed action index produces a learner that trains happily and drives into a wall.

The reading rule is the deterministic argmax from chapter 4, now over a row of the table. Nothing else in this chapter changes about how a policy is read. What changes is where the numbers come from.
lessons.task: Allocate the table with `q = {s: [0.0] * len(ACTIONS) for s in INNER}`, then finish `greedy(q, s)` so it returns `best = max(range(len(ACTIONS)), key=lambda a: q[s][a])`. The run scores the planned bearing of each cell one point and checks the reading gives that plan back.
lessons.hint: The entries are lists, so `q[s][a]` is the worth of bearing `a` in cell `s`.

value: q = {s: [0.0] * len(ACTIONS) for s in INNER}

lessons.title: The Rule That Learns Off Policy
lessons.goal: Apply the Q-learning update to a stream of transitions and watch a policy appear.
lessons.theory:
Q-learning is the TD update with one substitution: the target uses the **best** bearing available in the next cell, not the one the robot is about to take.

That single `max` is what makes it **off policy**. The behaviour can be as clumsy as you like, wandering, exploring, driving into walls, and the table still converges towards the value of the optimal policy, because the target never asks what the behaviour intends to do next. It is the property that lets a robot learn a good policy from a bad one, or from a log of somebody else driving.

The update is applied once per transition, in place, and nothing is stored. That is the whole algorithm, and it fits on one line.
lessons.task: Finish the update. Build the bootstrapped target with `target = r + GAMMA * (0.0 if done else max(q[nxt]))` and move the entry towards it with `q[s][a] = q[s][a] + ALPHA * (target - q[s][a])`. The agent explores at random, so the behaviour is deliberately bad.
lessons.hint: A terminal landing has no next row to maximise over, which is what the conditional is for.

value: target = r + GAMMA * (0.0 if done else max(q[nxt]))

lessons.title: Epsilon Buys Information
lessons.goal: Choose actions with an epsilon greedy rule and measure how often it explores.
lessons.theory:
A random behaviour learns everything slowly and a greedy behaviour learns nothing new. The standard compromise is **epsilon greedy**: with probability epsilon take a uniformly random bearing, otherwise take the current best.

Epsilon is a budget for information, paid in steps. At 0.1 the robot spends one move in ten deliberately doing something it does not believe in, which on hardware is one move in ten spent on purpose near a stair edge. That framing is worth keeping: exploration is not free curiosity, it is a line item.

Watch the number that comes back. The fraction of moves that leave the plan is not epsilon, it is three quarters of it, because one random draw in four lands back on the bearing the agent would have taken anyway. Quote the wrong one of those two in a report and your exploration budget is out by a third.
lessons.task: Finish `choose(q, s, epsilon, rng)` so that `if rng.random() < epsilon:` the whole body of that branch is `return rng.randrange(len(ACTIONS))`, and otherwise it returns the greedy bearing. Read the measured rates against the epsilons asked for.
lessons.hint: Draw the coin once per decision. Two draws per step give you an exploration rate you did not ask for.

lessons.title: Greedy Is Blind
lessons.goal: Show a zero exploration learner failing to find the dock at all.
lessons.theory:
An agent that always takes its current best bearing is not being efficient, it is being circular. It believes what it has seen, it only sees what it does, and it only does what it believes.

Start the table pessimistically, at a value below anything the arena can pay, and the loop closes hard. Trying a bearing raises its entry towards reality, which makes that bearing look better than the untried ones, so the agent tries it again. This is the trap that produces a robot which drives into the same corner for an hour.

The run trains the same learner at four exploration rates and reports whether the final greedy policy reaches the dock at all. This is not a subtle effect. It is the difference between a working robot and a hobbyist video.
lessons.task: Train at each exploration rate and count the outcomes. Count the successful training episodes with `if ends == DOCK:` inside the runner, and report whether the final greedy policy docks in `docks = final_end == DOCK`.
lessons.hint: The pessimistic start value is already set, and it is what turns a tried bearing into a preferred one.

lessons.title: Optimism Explores for Free
lessons.goal: Compare an optimistic and a pessimistic starting table by counting the pairs each one tried.
lessons.theory:
There is a way to explore without any randomness at all: start the table **above** what the arena can pay. Every bearing then looks better than it is, trying one drives its entry down towards the truth, and the untried bearings become the most attractive thing in the row. The agent sweeps the arena because it is disappointed, not because it is curious.

On this floor every reward except the dock is negative, so a table of zeros is already optimistic. Compare it against a table that starts at -30 and count the distinct state and bearing pairs each learner ever tried, out of `len(INNER) * len(ACTIONS)`.

Optimism is cheap, deterministic and repeatable, which makes it the first thing to try. Its limit is that it explores once: after the table has come down to reality it stops, so it handles a world that stands still and not a world that changes.
lessons.task: Count the coverage. Record each attempt with `tried.add((s, a))` and report the fraction as `covered = len(tried) / (len(INNER) * len(ACTIONS))`. Both learners run with no exploration at all.
lessons.hint: Record the pair the agent actually executed, inside the step loop, not the pair it would have preferred.

lessons.title: Cooling the Curiosity
lessons.goal: Decay exploration over training and count the falls it saves.
lessons.theory:
A fixed exploration rate is a fixed tax. Early in training it is the only reason anything is discovered; late in training it is a robot that already knows the way and still drives off the stairs one time in ten.

Decaying it fixes both ends. Start high enough to find the dock, fall towards a floor that keeps a little adaptability, and the usual schedule is geometric: multiply by a factor slightly below one after every episode, clipped at a minimum.

The measurement that matters here is not the final policy, because both settings will find it on a floor this small. It is the **damage taken on the way**, counted in episodes that ended over the stair edge. That column is the first honest number of this course about what training costs, and chapter 8 is built on it.
lessons.task: Add the schedule. After each episode set `epsilon = max(FLOOR, epsilon * DECAY)`, and count the episodes that ended badly with `falls = falls + 1`. Compare the fixed and decayed runs on falls, not on the final policy.
lessons.hint: Decay once per episode, not once per step, or the rate collapses before the first episode is over.

lessons.title: The Learning Rate Is a Bet
lessons.goal: Tune the learning rate on a slippery floor and find where a big step stops paying.
lessons.theory:
On a floor that never slips, a learning rate of 1.0 is correct. The target is exact, so overwriting the entry with it is not a gamble, it is an assignment.

Add slip and the target becomes one sample of a distribution. A rate of 1.0 now throws away everything the table knew in favour of whatever just happened, so the entry tracks the noise instead of the mean. The symptom is a **flickering policy**: bearings that keep changing long after the agent has learned the arena, which on a robot is a base that reverses in the same doorway forever.

So measure two things, not one. The score says whether the policy is any good; the flicker count says whether it has settled. On an arena this small the score barely separates the sensible rates, and the flicker count separates them by two orders of magnitude, which is the honest reason to prefer a small step.
lessons.task: Score each trained table. Run the evaluation episodes and average them with `mean_return = total / EVAL_EPISODES`, and report the best rate with `best_alpha = max(results, key=lambda row: row[1])[0]`.
lessons.hint: Evaluate with exploration off and a separate stream, or you are measuring the exploration and not the policy. The flicker counter is already wired into the training loop.

lessons.title: Does It Know the Answer
lessons.goal: Track how many bearings of the learned policy match the planner over training.
lessons.theory:
Return curves are noisy and they hide where a policy is still wrong. When you have a planner, there is a much sharper measurement available: compare the learned bearings against the planned ones, cell by cell, and count the matches.

This is a luxury of a small arena with a known model and you should use it while you have it. It tells you not only that the agent is improving but **which** cells it has not settled, and those cells are almost always the ones it rarely visits.

Expect the count to stall below the maximum, and do not panic at it. Print the gap between the best entry of a mismatched row and the entry of the planned bearing: when that gap is zero the two bearings are worth exactly the same and the disagreement is a tie, not an error. On this arena the start cell has two eight step routes to the dock, so the learner is entitled to prefer either one.

A real mismatch has a gap. That is the number to look at, not the count.
lessons.task: Take the measurement at each checkpoint: count matches with `agree = sum(1 for s in INNER if greedy(q, s) == PLANNED[s])`, and find the stragglers with `wrong = [s for s in INNER if greedy(q, s) != PLANNED[s]]`. Then read the gap column underneath before you call any of them a mistake.
lessons.hint: Keep training the same table between checkpoints instead of restarting, or the curve you print is not a learning curve.

value: agree = sum(1 for s in INNER if greedy(q, s) == PLANNED[s])
wrong = [s for s in INNER if greedy(q, s) != PLANNED[s]]

lessons.title: The Curve of Competence
lessons.goal: Plot a learning curve from training returns and separate it from the greedy score.
lessons.theory:
There are two curves and confusing them is the most common reporting error in this field.

The **training return** is what the robot collected while exploring, so it carries the cost of every deliberate mistake and it can never reach the optimum while epsilon is above zero. The **greedy return** is what the current table would do with exploration switched off, which is the number a deployed robot would actually get.

Report both. A training curve that flattens below the optimum is usually not a stuck learner, it is the exploration tax, and a team that reads it as failure will spend a week tuning the wrong thing. The gap between the two curves is roughly what your epsilon costs per episode.

And average over several learners. A single run on an arena this small jumps from hopeless to optimal inside one block, so the curve you would print is a step and it tells you nothing about the shape of learning. Eight independent learners with eight seeds give a curve you can read.
lessons.task: Build both curves. Accumulate each learner with `block_total = block_total + episode_total`, then close the block across the eight of them with `curve.append(train_sum / RUNS)` and store the averaged greedy score alongside it.
lessons.hint: Each learner keeps its own stream and its own table across blocks, so build the eight of them once, before the block loop.

lessons.title: On Policy, On the Hook
lessons.goal: Implement SARSA and see it learn the value of the behaviour it is actually running.
lessons.theory:
Q-learning bootstraps on the best bearing available next. **SARSA** bootstraps on the bearing it is actually going to take, which it has to choose before it can update.

That is the whole difference and it changes what the table means. Q-learning learns the value of the optimal policy while behaving badly; SARSA learns the value of the epsilon greedy policy it is running, exploration mistakes included. Its name is the five things it needs: state, action, reward, next state, next action.

So SARSA is the algorithm that knows it is going to be clumsy. When the cost of a clumsy move is a broken robot rather than a lost point, that self awareness stops being a technicality, which is what the next lesson measures.
lessons.task: Finish SARSA. When the run continues, pick the follow up bearing before updating with `nxt_a = choose(q, nxt, EPSILON, rng)`, then apply `q[s][a] = q[s][a] + ALPHA * (r + GAMMA * (0.0 if done else q[nxt][nxt_a]) - q[s][a])` and carry that bearing into the next turn.
lessons.hint: A terminal cell has no row in the table, so only ask for a follow up bearing when the episode is still alive.

value: q[s][a] = q[s][a] + ALPHA * (r + GAMMA * (0.0 if done else q[nxt][nxt_a]) - q[s][a])

lessons.title: The Cliff
lessons.goal: Train both learners on a cliff walk and read the two different routes they choose.
lessons.theory:
The arena moves to a service corridor: four rows by twelve columns, the robot starts at the bottom left, the charging point is at the bottom right, and the whole bottom row between them is an unguarded loading dock edge. Going over it costs 100 and puts the robot back at the start.

The shortest route runs along the second row, one cell above the drop, twelve columns long. The safe route climbs another row first and pays two extra steps for the distance.

Q-learning learns the values of the optimal policy, and the optimal policy does not explore, so it settles on the edge route. SARSA learns the value of what it is actually doing, which includes a random bearing one time in ten, and next to a drop that possibility is worth avoiding, so it settles higher up. Both are correct answers to different questions, and the printed routes are the two questions.
lessons.task: Walk each trained table with the greedy policy: record the route with `path.append(cell)` and reduce it to one number with `top_row = min(cell[0] for cell in path)`. Row 2 is the edge route, anything smaller is the safe one.
lessons.hint: The two learners share every hyperparameter, so if the routes come out identical, check that the SARSA update is not maximising.

value: top_row = min(cell[0] for cell in path)

lessons.title: What Falls Cost While Learning
lessons.goal: Count the cliff entries each learner pays for during training, not after it.
lessons.theory:
The previous lesson compared the two final routes and Q-learning won on paper: its route is two steps shorter. That comparison is the one every tutorial makes and it prices only the answer, never the search.

So price the search. Count how many times the robot actually went over the edge during training, and the ranking inverts: the learner whose route hugs the drop is also the learner that spent training falling off it, because its behaviour policy explores next to a hundred point penalty.

This is the number to carry into the next chapter. On a screen a cliff entry is a reset and a -100; in a warehouse it is a robot on its back at the bottom of a loading dock, and no amount of shorter route pays for one of them.
lessons.task: Count the falls. A transition over the edge is the one where `if r < -50.0:` holds, so increment `cliff_falls = cliff_falls + 1` there and report the total for each learner together with its mean training return.
lessons.hint: Count inside the step loop, not at the end of the episode, because one episode can go over the edge several times.

lessons.title: The Floor Fights Back
lessons.goal: Compare two policies that tie on a dry floor and separate as the floor gets slippier.
lessons.theory:
Two routes leave the start cell and reach the dock in eight steps. The planned one from chapter 4 climbs the left column and crosses the top row. The timid one runs along the bottom row and up the right column. On a floor that never slips they are worth exactly the same, 3.0, and no measurement can separate them.

Add slip and they are not the same policy at all. The timid route passes through the cell below the stair edge, so one sideways slip there ends the run on the floor below; the planned route is shielded by shelving on both sides of its exposed cell, and no single slip along it can reach the hazard at all.

That is the shape of risk in a plan: it is a property of the geometry the route touches, it is invisible at zero noise, and it grows faster than the noise does because a route gets a fresh draw at every exposed cell. A plan validated on a dry floor tells you very little about a dusty one.
lessons.task: Run the planned policy at each slip level and count the outcomes. Add up the failures with `fell = fell + 1` when the run ends on the stair edge, and reduce them with `fall_rate = fell / EPISODES`.
lessons.hint: Neither policy changes in this lesson. Only the floor does, which is the point of it.

lessons.title: Risk Lives in the Tail
lessons.goal: Report a policy by its worst outcomes as well as its mean return.
lessons.theory:
Every method in this course optimises an **expectation**, and an expectation is a bad summary of a robot. A policy that docks nicely 95 times and falls down the stairs 5 times has a respectable mean and has destroyed five robots.

So report the distribution, not the average. The cheapest useful version is three numbers: the mean, the fraction of runs below some acceptable line, and the worst run seen. Those take four lines of code and they are what a safety review will ask for.

This is also where the difference between the two learners from earlier becomes a decision rather than a preference. Compare the mean of a route and its tail: two policies with almost the same mean can have tails an order of magnitude apart, and the tail is the one that shows up in the incident report.
lessons.task: Summarise each policy properly. Sort the sampled returns and read the low end with `tail = ordered[int(0.05 * len(ordered))]`, then count the disasters with `bad = sum(1 for g in returns if g < ACCEPTABLE)`.
lessons.hint: Sort a copy of the list before indexing into it, and use the same seeded episodes for every policy so the comparison is fair.

value: bad = sum(1 for g in returns if g < ACCEPTABLE)

lessons.title: Shaping Without Lying
lessons.goal: Add a potential based bonus that speeds up learning and provably cannot change the optimum.
lessons.theory:
Sparse reward is the reason a learner wanders for a thousand episodes before anything happens. Extra reward for progress fixes that and usually breaks the task, as chapter 0 measured.

There is one form that cannot break it. Pick any function of the state, call it the **potential**, and pay the difference `GAMMA * potential(next) - potential(here)` on every transition. Because the payments telescope along any path, every route to the dock gains exactly the same total, so the ranking of policies is untouched. The optimal policy is provably the same one, and the learner reaches it sooner because the signal now arrives every step instead of once.

Use the negative distance to the dock as the potential and measure two things: the episodes needed to reach the planned policy, and whether the policy it lands on is still that one. Both learners then keep training to the same budget, so the final tables are comparable. Both columns matter: speed with a changed optimum is not a win.
lessons.task: Add the shaping term. Compute it with `shaped = r + GAMMA * potential(nxt) - potential(s)` and use it as the reward inside the update. Then divide the two episode counts with `speedup = results[False] / results[True]` and check the learned policy still matches the plan.
lessons.hint: The potential is a function of the cell only. If it ever looks at the bearing, the proof does not hold and the guarantee is gone.

lessons.title: Shaping That Lies
lessons.goal: Let a learner discover the loitering exploit that a hand written bonus creates.
lessons.theory:
Chapter 0 hand wrote a policy that farmed a proximity bonus and showed it scored better than docking. That was a demonstration you had to build. This one the agent finds on its own.

Pay `NEAR_BONUS` for every step that ends next to the dock, with no matching subtraction, and let Q-learning optimise. It will, exactly as written, and the table it produces sends the robot to the cell beside the dock and keeps it there until the step budget runs out. Nobody chose that behaviour and nobody reviewed it, because it never appeared in the code as an instruction.

The measurement that exposes it is to score the learned policy under the **true** reward, without the bonus. That gap between what the learner optimised and what you wanted is the whole failure mode, and printing both numbers side by side is the cheapest audit there is.
lessons.task: Score the exploit. Count how many evaluation runs never terminate with `stalled = sum(1 for outcome in outcomes if outcome is None)`, and score the policy on the honest reward with `true_score = total_true / RUNS`.
lessons.hint: The bonus is added during training only. Evaluation has to use the plain arena reward or you are grading the exploit with the same ruler that created it.

value: stalled = sum(1 for outcome in outcomes if outcome is None)

lessons.title: Freezing the Policy
lessons.goal: Separate training mode from deployment and count what leaving exploration on costs.
lessons.theory:
A trained agent has two switches that must both go off before it leaves the lab: the exploration rate and the learning rate. Leaving either on is a deployment that keeps experimenting on the customer.

Exploration is the expensive one. A deployed robot at epsilon 0.05 takes a deliberately wrong bearing one move in twenty, forever, and near a stair edge that is not a rounding error, it is a schedule of accidents. Leaving the learning rate on is subtler and worse in a different way: the table keeps drifting on whatever the robot happens to see, with nobody watching the curve.

So freezing is a step in the pipeline, not a detail. The run deploys one frozen table at five exploration rates over a thousand runs each, which is a couple of shifts for a warehouse robot, and reports both columns that matter. The step count rises from the first row onwards, because exploration always costs time. The incident count stays at zero for a while and then does not, because this route is shielded by shelving until the exploration is wide enough to leave it.
lessons.task: Deploy the frozen table at each rate and count. Increment `crashes = crashes + 1` when a run ends on the stair edge, and report the incidents per thousand runs with `per_thousand = 1000.0 * crashes / RUNS`.
lessons.hint: Train once, then evaluate the same table three times. Retraining per rate would measure something else entirely.

lessons.title: Confident About Nothing
lessons.goal: Find the cells where the learned policy is a tie break pretending to be a decision.
lessons.theory:
A table cannot say it does not know. Ask it for the bearing in a cell it has never visited and it answers, immediately, with whatever the tie break rule produces, and nothing in the interface distinguishes that answer from one backed by ten thousand visits.

This is not a small corner of the arena early in training. Count the cells whose row is still untouched after a short run and you will find the agent is guessing over a serious fraction of the floor, with total confidence, in exactly the places it has least reason to be right.

The fix is to carry the visit counts alongside the table and refuse to act below a threshold, handing control back to a scripted fallback. That is the seed of the shield built in the next chapter, and it starts here with an honest count of what the agent has actually seen.
lessons.task: Audit the table. Collect the unsure cells with `unsure = [s for s in INNER if visits[s] < MIN_VISITS]` and the untouched rows with `untouched = [s for s in INNER if max(q[s]) == 0.0 and min(q[s]) == 0.0]`, then read what fraction of the arena the policy is guessing on.
lessons.hint: Count a visit when the robot stands on the cell, so a cell it has only ever seen from the outside still counts as unseen.

value: unsure = [s for s in INNER if visits[s] < MIN_VISITS]
untouched = [s for s in INNER if max(q[s]) == 0.0 and min(q[s]) == 0.0]

lessons.title: Counting the Lives It Spends
lessons.goal: Instrument training to report the episodes, the steps and the falls a solution cost.
lessons.theory:
Every chapter so far reported what the agent learned. None of them reported what learning cost, and that omission is the reason people believe a robot can be trained by trial and error.

So instrument it. Three counters, kept during training and reported at the end: **episodes**, because each one is a reset and somebody has to perform it; **steps**, because each one is a physical move; and **falls**, because each one is the robot on the floor below.

Run it on twelve seeds and report the median, not one run. A single training run is one sample of a very skewed distribution and quoting it is how projects end up with a plan built on the luckiest number anyone saw. The arena is five cells by five, the floor slips one time in ten, and the task is to drive eight cells. Read what that costs before you read anything else.
lessons.task: Add the counters to the training loop. Charge every transition with `cost["steps"] = cost["steps"] + 1`, and charge a fall with `cost["falls"] = cost["falls"] + 1` whenever the robot lands on the stair edge. The episode counter is already there.
lessons.hint: Count the fall on the transition that lands there, not at the end of the episode, and the two counts happen to agree here only because a fall ends the run.

lessons.title: From Steps to Hours
lessons.goal: Convert a training budget into robot time using the speed of a real base.
lessons.theory:
A step is not a unit of anything until you attach a robot to it. A Kobuki class base crosses a 40 cm tile in about `SECONDS_PER_MOVE` seconds including the settle, and an episode reset means somebody carries the robot back to the start, which is `RESET_SECONDS` if the somebody is standing right there and much more if they are not.

Multiply and the abstraction becomes a schedule. Notice which term dominates: on a task this short the resets cost more than the driving, which is why every hardware reinforcement learning paper has a paragraph about automatic reset mechanisms and why most of them build one.

The number that comes out of this lesson is small, and it should be. Five cells by five, eight steps to the dock, no obstacles worth the name. Keep it, because the next two lessons multiply it by things that are not small.
lessons.task: Convert the budget. Compute the robot time with `seconds = steps * SECONDS_PER_MOVE + episodes * RESET_SECONDS`, turn it into `hours = seconds / 3600.0`, and report the share of it that is resets rather than driving.
lessons.hint: Both terms are needed. Reporting only the driving time is how a two day experiment gets scheduled for an afternoon.
lessons.starter:
import random
import statistics

ROWS = 5
COLS = 5
START = (4, 0)
DOCK = (0, 4)
HAZARD = (2, 2)
WALLS = ((1, 1), (1, 3), (3, 1), (3, 3))
ACTIONS = ((-1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1))
NAMES = ("north", "east", "south", "west")

def move(cell, action):
    r = cell[0] + ACTIONS[action][0]
    c = cell[1] + ACTIONS[action][1]
    if r < 0 or r >= ROWS or c < 0 or c >= COLS:
        return cell
    if (r, c) in WALLS:
        return cell
    return (r, c)

def step(cell, action):
    nxt = move(cell, action)
    if nxt == DOCK:
        return nxt, 10.0, True
    if nxt == HAZARD:
        return nxt, -20.0, True
    return nxt, -1.0, False

def cells():
    return [(r, c) for r in range(ROWS) for c in range(COLS) if (r, c) not in WALLS]

def terminal(cell):
    return cell == DOCK or cell == HAZARD

INNER = [c for c in cells() if not terminal(c)]

PLANNED = {
    (0, 0): 1, (0, 1): 1, (0, 2): 1, (0, 3): 1,
    (1, 0): 0, (1, 2): 0, (1, 4): 0,
    (2, 0): 0, (2, 1): 3, (2, 3): 1, (2, 4): 0,
    (3, 0): 0, (3, 2): 2, (3, 4): 0,
    (4, 0): 0, (4, 1): 1, (4, 2): 1, (4, 3): 1, (4, 4): 0,
}

SLIP = 0.1
PERPENDICULAR = ((3, 1), (0, 2), (1, 3), (2, 0))

def sample_step(cell, action, rng):
    executed = action
    if rng.random() < SLIP:
        executed = rng.choice(PERPENDICULAR[action])
    return step(cell, executed)

def exact_values(policy, gamma, threshold=1e-13, limit=40000):
    side = SLIP / 2.0
    v = {c: 0.0 for c in cells()}
    for _ in range(limit):
        delta = 0.0
        for s in INNER:
            before = v[s]
            a = policy[s]
            total = 0.0
            for executed, prob in ((a, 1.0 - SLIP), (PERPENDICULAR[a][0], side), (PERPENDICULAR[a][1], side)):
                nxt, r, done = step(s, executed)
                total = total + prob * (r + gamma * (0.0 if done else v[nxt]))
            v[s] = total
            delta = max(delta, abs(v[s] - before))
        if delta < threshold:
            break
    return v

def greedy(q, s):
    return max(range(len(ACTIONS)), key=lambda a: q[s][a])

def new_table():
    return {s: [0.0] * len(ACTIONS) for s in INNER}

def greedy_return(q, max_steps=40):
    cell = START
    total = 0.0
    for _ in range(max_steps):
        cell, r, done = step(cell, greedy(q, cell))
        total = total + r
        if done:
            break
    return total

SECONDS_PER_MOVE = 0.4
RESET_SECONDS = 12.0
REPAIR_USD = 180.0
FALL_MINUTES = 45.0
SHIFT_HOURS = 8.0
OPTIMAL_RETURN = 3.0
STREAK = 20

GAMMA = 0.95
ALPHA = 0.3
EPSILON = 0.2

def train_until_solved(seed, limit=6000):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    q = new_table()
    cost = {"episodes": 0, "steps": 0, "falls": 0}
    streak = 0
    for _ in range(limit):
        cost["episodes"] = cost["episodes"] + 1
        s = START
        for _ in range(60):
            a = rng.randrange(len(ACTIONS)) if rng.random() < EPSILON else greedy(q, s)
            nxt, r, done = sample_step(s, a, rng)
            cost["steps"] = cost["steps"] + 1
            if nxt == HAZARD:
                cost["falls"] = cost["falls"] + 1
            target = r + GAMMA * (0.0 if done else max(q[nxt]))
            q[s][a] = q[s][a] + ALPHA * (target - q[s][a])
            s = nxt
            if done:
                break
        if greedy_return(q) == OPTIMAL_RETURN:
            streak = streak + 1
        else:
            streak = 0
        if streak >= STREAK:
            break
    return q, cost

SEEDS = 12

runs = [train_until_solved(100 + s)[1] for s in range(SEEDS)]
episodes = int(statistics.median(r["episodes"] for r in runs))
steps = int(statistics.median(r["steps"] for r in runs))
seconds = 0.0
hours = 0.0
# TODO: robot time, then hours
reset_share = 0.0
if seconds:
    reset_share = episodes * RESET_SECONDS / seconds
print("median episodes", episodes, "median steps", steps)
print("robot seconds", round(seconds, 1), "hours", round(hours, 3))
print("share of the time spent on resets", round(reset_share, 3))
print("shifts of", SHIFT_HOURS, "hours", round(hours / SHIFT_HOURS, 3))

lessons.title: The Repair Bill
lessons.goal: Price the falls of a training run in parts and technician time.
lessons.theory:
A fall in the arena is a number on a screen. A fall on hardware is a robot that went over an unguarded edge, which in the fleet this course is written against means a cracked lidar mount, a bent bumper bracket, and a technician who stops what they were doing.

Price it honestly and conservatively: `REPAIR_USD` for the parts of a typical drop and `FALL_MINUTES` of somebody's afternoon. Do not model the low probability outcomes, the drop onto a person or the battery puncture, because the point is made without them.

Then read the total against the twelve seeds. The bill is not the median run, it is the sum, because a team training a policy runs the experiment more than once. That is the number that goes on the slide next to the words trial and error.
lessons.task: Price the damage. Compute `repair = falls * REPAIR_USD` and the labour as `technician_hours = falls * FALL_MINUTES / 60.0`, for the median run and for the whole set of seeds.
lessons.hint: Sum the falls over the seeds for the fleet number, and use the median for the per run number. They are answers to different questions.

lessons.title: Every State Wants Visits
lessons.goal: Grow the arena and measure how the training cost scales with the size of the table.
lessons.theory:
A tabular learner has to visit every state and bearing pair enough times to average out the noise. There is no sharing between cells: what it learns about one tile teaches it nothing about the tile next to it.

So the cost grows with the table, and it grows faster than the table does. The pairs multiply, and on top of that the robot has to walk further to reach the new ones, so the steps per pair rise as well. That second factor is the one people forget when they estimate a bigger problem by scaling their prototype linearly.

Measure it on open grids from four cells across to twelve, with the same learner and the same criterion, and print the steps per pair alongside the totals. Two columns grow. That is the whole argument for function approximation, and it is the honest reason this course stops at tables.
lessons.task: Report the scaling. Compute the table size with `pairs = len(cells) * len(ACTIONS)` and the intensity with `per_pair = steps / pairs`, for every grid size.
lessons.hint: The optimal route on an open grid of side `n` is `2 * (n - 1)` steps, which is what the solved test compares against.
lessons.starter:
import random
import statistics

ACTIONS = ((-1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1))
GAMMA = 0.97
ALPHA = 0.3
EPSILON = 0.2
SEEDS = 5

def make_arena(n):
    start = (n - 1, 0)
    goal = (0, n - 1)
    hazard = (n // 2, n // 2)
    cells = [(r, c) for r in range(n) for c in range(n)]

    def step_n(cell, a):
        r = cell[0] + ACTIONS[a][0]
        c = cell[1] + ACTIONS[a][1]
        if r < 0 or r >= n or c < 0 or c >= n:
            r, c = cell
        if (r, c) == goal:
            return (r, c), 10.0, True
        if (r, c) == hazard:
            return (r, c), -20.0, True
        return (r, c), -1.0, False

    return start, goal, cells, step_n

def solve(n, seed, limit=100000):
    start, goal, cells, step_n = make_arena(n)
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    q = {s: [0.0] * len(ACTIONS) for s in cells}
    best = 2 * (n - 1)
    steps = 0
    for episode in range(1, limit + 1):
        s = start
        for _ in range(20 * n):
            a = rng.randrange(len(ACTIONS)) if rng.random() < EPSILON else max(range(len(ACTIONS)), key=lambda x: q[s][x])
            nxt, r, done = step_n(s, a)
            steps = steps + 1
            target = r + GAMMA * (0.0 if done else max(q[nxt]))
            q[s][a] = q[s][a] + ALPHA * (target - q[s][a])
            s = nxt
            if done:
                break
        cell = start
        walked = 0
        for _ in range(20 * n):
            cell, r, done = step_n(cell, max(range(len(ACTIONS)), key=lambda x: q[cell][x]))
            walked = walked + 1
            if done:
                break
        if cell == goal and walked == best:
            return episode, steps, cells
    return limit, steps, cells

for n in (4, 6, 8, 10, 12):
    results = [solve(n, s) for s in range(SEEDS)]
    episodes = statistics.median(r[0] for r in results)
    steps = statistics.median(r[1] for r in results)
    cells = results[0][2]
    pairs = 0
    per_pair = 0.0
    # TODO: the size of the table and the steps spent per entry
    print("side", n, "cells", len(cells), "pairs", pairs, "episodes", episodes,
          "steps", steps, "steps per pair", round(per_pair, 2))

lessons.title: The Arm That Cannot Be Tabled
lessons.goal: Extrapolate the tabular budget to a jointed arm and read the answer in robot years.
lessons.theory:
The previous lesson measured how many steps a table entry costs. This one takes that number somewhere it does not want to go.

Discretise a six joint arm at ten positions per joint and the state space is ten to the sixth. Give it two bearings per joint and the table has twelve million entries. At the twenty visits per entry the arena needed, and 0.4 seconds per move, the training budget is measured in **years of continuous robot time**, on a machine that costs more per hour than the ceiling it hangs from.

That is why nobody trains a manipulator with a table, and it is also why the answer is not a bigger computer. The fix is to stop storing one number per state: a function approximator shares what it learns between nearby configurations, which is what the deep methods buy and the only thing they buy. Everything else in this course still applies to them, including the falls.
lessons.task: Extrapolate. Compute the state count with `states = bins ** joints`, and turn the whole table into time with `robot_years = pairs * VISITS_PER_PAIR * SECONDS_PER_MOVE / SECONDS_PER_YEAR`. Read the row for six joints at ten bins.
lessons.hint: One bearing pair per joint means the action count is twice the joints, which is generous: a real arm also has speeds.

lessons.title: A Shield Before a Policy
lessons.goal: Filter unsafe bearings with a one step model and measure what the filter costs and saves.
lessons.theory:
The learner is allowed to be ignorant. It is not allowed to be ignorant about the stairs.

A **shield** sits between the policy and the actuators and removes bearings that a one step model says can end badly. It is not learned, it is written, and it comes from the same place a safety case does: a geometric fact about the floor plan. Crucially it must consider what the floor can do, not only what the command says: on a slippery floor a bearing is unsafe if **any** of its possible landings is the stair edge, not only the commanded one.

The trade is real and it should be measured, not assumed. The shield removes the falls completely, and it also slows learning down, because the agent never gets to find out what is wrong with the middle of the arena and spends more steps wandering around a place it is forbidden to understand. Both columns go in the report.
lessons.task: Build the shield. Keep the bearings whose landings are all safe with `allowed = [a for a in range(len(ACTIONS)) if HAZARD not in landings(s, a)]`, explore inside that list, and exploit inside it with `a = max(allowed, key=lambda x: q[s][x])`.
lessons.hint: If every bearing in a cell is unsafe, fall back to the full list rather than crashing. On this arena that never happens, and on a real floor plan it will.

value: allowed = [a for a in range(len(ACTIONS)) if HAZARD not in landings(s, a)]

lessons.title: Learning From Someone Who Knows
lessons.goal: Warm start a table from teleoperated demonstrations and measure the falls it saves.
lessons.theory:
Nobody sensible starts a robot from a table of zeros. Somebody drives it, badly and by hand, for twenty runs, and the learner updates on those transitions before it ever chooses a bearing of its own.

The demonstrations do not have to be optimal and they do not have to be complete. What they buy is the first arrival at the dock, which is the event a random learner spends most of its budget waiting for, and every update after it has a real value to bootstrap from.

Measure two savings and report both. Episodes to solve fall by about half, which is convenience. Falls fall too, which is a robot that did not break, and unlike the first number that one has a price attached from lesson three.
lessons.task: Add the warm start. Drive the demonstration episodes with the teacher bearing `a = PLANNED[s]`, updating the table on those transitions, then let the learner take over. Report the saving as `saved = plain_falls - warm_falls`.
lessons.hint: Charge the demonstration steps and any demonstration falls to the same counters. A teleoperated run costs robot time too.
lessons.starter:
import random
import statistics

ROWS = 5
COLS = 5
START = (4, 0)
DOCK = (0, 4)
HAZARD = (2, 2)
WALLS = ((1, 1), (1, 3), (3, 1), (3, 3))
ACTIONS = ((-1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1))
NAMES = ("north", "east", "south", "west")

def move(cell, action):
    r = cell[0] + ACTIONS[action][0]
    c = cell[1] + ACTIONS[action][1]
    if r < 0 or r >= ROWS or c < 0 or c >= COLS:
        return cell
    if (r, c) in WALLS:
        return cell
    return (r, c)

def step(cell, action):
    nxt = move(cell, action)
    if nxt == DOCK:

lessons.title: The Simulator Is Not the Floor
lessons.goal: Train at one slip level, deploy at three, and measure both directions of the mismatch.
lessons.theory:
Training in simulation removes the falls, the resets and the years. It introduces one problem in their place: the simulator is wrong, and the policy is optimal for the simulator.

The corridor from earlier in this chapter shows it in both directions, which is the part usually left out. A policy trained on a perfectly dry floor takes the route along the edge, and deployed on a dusty one it goes over three times per run. A policy trained only at heavy slip learns a route that depends on being pushed around, and deployed on a dry floor it deadlocks in a two cell cycle and never arrives at all: its run ends at the 200 step cap with the goal untouched.

**Domain randomisation** trains across a spread of slip levels instead of one. It is worse than the dry policy on the dry floor, by two steps, and it is the only row of the table that arrives everywhere. That trade, a little worse everywhere against catastrophic somewhere, is the whole argument, and here it is three lines of output rather than a slogan.
lessons.task: Build the matrix. Score every policy on every floor, reduce the crashes with `fall_rate = falls / RUNS`, and compare the two mismatches with `gap = wrong_floor - right_floor`. Read the arrival column as carefully as the fall column.
lessons.hint: Use the same evaluation seed for every cell of the matrix so the rows are comparable, and a different one from training.

lessons.title: The Honest Verdict
lessons.goal: Put every measured cost into one comparison and let the arithmetic pick the plan.
lessons.theory:
The chapter has produced numbers instead of opinions, so the conclusion can be arithmetic instead of advice.

On one side, training on hardware: the median steps and episodes from lesson one, priced at robot time and repairs. On the other, training in simulation and transferring: the same learning happens at no physical cost, and what remains is a short shielded run on the real robot to close the gap the simulator left.

Compute both and print the verdict. The point is not that simulation wins, which it obviously does on this arena. It is that the margin is a number you can defend, and that the same table tells you the one thing simulation cannot buy: the shielded fine tuning at the end is not optional, because the fall rate of a policy that has never touched the real floor is measured, in the previous lesson, and it is not zero.

lessons.title: The Arena Specification
lessons.goal: Build the project arena and prove by search that the task is possible before training anything.
lessons.theory:
The project arena is a six by seven service bay. The robot starts in the bottom left corner, the charging dock is the top right cell, six shelving units block the middle, and there are **two** unguarded edges rather than one. The floor slips 15 times in a hundred, the dock pays 20, an edge costs 30, and every move costs 1.

Before a single episode runs, verify the task. A breadth first search from the start cell, refusing to enter a hazard, answers two questions that no amount of training will answer for you: is the dock reachable at all, and is any cell of the bay cut off by the shelving.

This check takes ten lines and it is the difference between debugging a learner for a day and reading a printed number. An agent that cannot solve an impossible arena looks exactly like an agent with a bug in its update rule.
lessons.task: Finish the search. Expand each neighbour by recording its distance with `distance[nxt] = distance[cell] + 1` and queueing it with `frontier.append(nxt)`. Then read the distance to the dock and the count of cells the search never reached.
lessons.hint: A hazard is a legal cell to fall into and an illegal cell to route through, so the search must refuse to expand from one.

lessons.title: The Ground Truth
lessons.goal: Solve the project arena with value iteration to produce the benchmark the learner will be graded against.
lessons.theory:
You have a model of this arena, so use it. Value iteration under the slip distribution produces the optimal value of every cell and the optimal bearing to take there, and those numbers become the yardstick for everything that follows.

This is not what a robot would do. It is what an engineer does before letting a robot loose, and having the answer in advance is the only reason the rest of the project can say anything precise about how well the learner did. Without a benchmark, a learning curve that flattens is either success or failure and you cannot tell which.

Print the value at the start cell and the arrow map. Check the arrows against the floor plan from the previous lesson: the optimal route climbs the left column and crosses the top row, and it does not go near either edge.

lessons.hint: `expected` already averages over the commanded bearing and the two slips, so the sweep only has to maximise it.

lessons.theory:
Now the agent, with no model and no map. Q-learning, epsilon greedy starting at 0.5 and cooling towards a floor, and a stopping rule that asks the only question that matters: does the greedy policy drive the optimal eleven step route to the dock.

The cost counters from chapter 8 come along, because a training run that does not report what it spent is half a result. Read all four numbers: episodes, steps, falls, and the agreement with the planner.

Expect the agreement to stop short of every cell, and expect that to be fine. The agent always starts in the same corner, so the far side of the bay gets visited rarely and its bearings stay near whatever they were initialised to. Those cells do not matter for this task and they would matter enormously if the start ever moved, which is a sentence worth keeping for the deployment review.

The previous lesson produced a working policy and a body count. This one removes the body count.

The shield is the same one as chapter 8, adapted to two hazards: a bearing is refused if the commanded landing **or either slip landing** is an edge. It is written from the floor plan, it is not learned, and it is checked before every move including the exploratory ones.

Measure both sides over eight seeds. The falls go to zero, which is the whole point. The steps go up by most of half again, because the agent is now forbidden from ever finding out what is wrong with the middle of the bay, so it wanders longer before its table settles. That extra time is the price of the guarantee, it is measurable, and it is much cheaper than the alternative.

lessons.title: The Evaluation Bench
lessons.goal: Score four deployment configurations and find the one that is unsafe.
lessons.theory:
Two tables have been trained and each can be deployed with the shield on or off, which is four configurations, and they are not four flavours of the same thing.

The bench runs 500 seeded episodes of each and reports the arrival rate, the fall rate, the mean return and the fifth percentile. Run it before reading the next paragraph, because the interesting row is not the one anyone expects.

The policy trained **behind** the shield is the dangerous one to deploy **without** it. It never fell during training, so it never learned that the middle of the bay is fatal, and the values it holds there are the innocent numbers it started with. Take the shield away at deployment and it drives into an edge in about one run in twenty. A safety mechanism used during training becomes part of the trained artefact, and shipping the table without it ships something that was never tested.

The first two rows come out identical to the last digit, and that is also information: the table trained in the open already refuses to go near an edge, so switching the shield on changes nothing it was going to do. A shield that costs nothing on a policy that has learned the danger is the cheapest insurance in the report.

lessons.goal: Freeze the policy and print an acceptance card that decides go or hold from the measurements.
lessons.theory:
The last artefact of the project is not the table. It is the card that says what the table is, what it was measured to do, and under what conditions it may be switched on.

Everything on it has already been measured in this chapter: the benchmark from the planner, the arrival and fall rates from the bench, the training cost from the damage report. The card adds two things and no opinions. First it **freezes** the policy, exploration and learning both off, into a plain lookup that has no way to change itself. Second it applies acceptance thresholds and lets the arithmetic answer.

Read the last column carefully. One configuration is refused, and it is the one that would have shipped if the review had only looked at the training falls.
